name: The dual offspring of Philosophical Radicalism: Darwinism and Socialism
plain_explanation: Bentham's school, though it saw itself as a single unified movement, in fact planted the seeds of two very different later movements: Darwinian 'survival of the fittest,' extending Malthusian free competition to all of life, and Socialism, drawn out by critics of Ricardo's labour theory of value.
precise_definition: Russell's historical claim that the Philosophical Radicals were 'a transitional school' whose economic doctrines (Malthusian population theory, Ricardian labour-value theory) gave rise, on one branch, to Darwin's theory of evolution by unregulated struggle, and, on another, to the Socialism of Hodgskin and Owen.
why_it_mattered: It explains why the mid-nineteenth-century intellectual landscape splits from a common Radical root into camps that appear at first opposed.
historical_origin: Ricardo's 1817 labour theory of value; Malthus's theory of population; Darwin's Origin of Species (1859).
examples: Thomas Hodgskin's 1825 pamphlet Labour Defended Against the Claims of Capital
The first recorded use of the word 'Socialist' in 1827, applied to followers of Robert Owen
influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates the chapter on Karl Marx that immediately follows, in which Socialism 'acquired a philosophy.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political and economic in origin.
